title: The Long History of Chocolate

paragraphs.text: In San Francisco, half a dozen men and women race around a tiny chocolate factory, checking temperature settings, sorting beans and operating machinery. This is the home of Dandelion Chocolate, a small-batch chocolate maker founded in 2010 by two former tech entrepreneurs. The tools and flavors have changed, but the work of roasting and grinding cacao beans, and mixing them with a few simple ingredients to create a fantastic food, is a practice that goes back to early Mesoamerican civilizations. The Olmec people of southern Mexico were probably the first to roast and grind cacao beans for drinks, possibly as early as 1500 B.C., says Hayes Lavis, a cultural arts curator for the National Museum of the American Indian. Although there is no written history for the Olmecs, he explains that scientists tested pots and vessels uncovered from this ancient civilization, and discovered traces of the chemical theobromine which is found in cacao, and therefore also chocolate.

In their raw state, cacao seeds are very bitter. They need to go through fermentation — a chemical change caused by natural sugar — before they can be eaten. 'How would you think to take the seed, harvest it, dry it, let it ferment, and roast it? It's not something you would normally think to do,' Lavis said. Perhaps, he suggests, people were eating the fruit and spitting seeds into the fire, and their rich aroma inspired the thought that 'maybe there's something more we could do with this.' The Olmec cacao drink, however, would probably be unrecognizable to today's hot chocolate drinkers. 'Seldom did they add any sweetener — once in a while honey, but mainly to try to ferment it,' says anthropologist Joel Palka. He explains, however, that a variety of herbs were available to the Olmecs for seasoning cacao-based food and drink. 'There were dozens of things that would be used to flavor it,' he says, ranging from chili and vanilla to magnolia.

In traditional preparation methods, still used by some small-scale producers, farmers take seeds out of the pods and ferment them in banana leaves. In more modern methods, the seeds are fermented in raised wooden boxes that enable air to pass through, which gives more consistent results. Dandelion Chocolate acquires beans that have been fermented for several days and then dried. While the company pours dried beans into a coffee roasting machine, in the past all cacao roasters would have simply placed beans on a fire. 'They'll get almost burnt,' founder Todd Masonis says.

In Mesoamerica, cacao was seen as a sacred food, and a means of reinforcing the social bonds between all the tribes that lived in the area, and also between immediate and extended families. Cacao drinks in Mesoamerica also became associated with high status and special occasions, Palka says. Special occasions might include initiation rites for young men, or celebrations marking the point when the Maya year finished, sometime during winter.

Paintings recovered from this time show cacao being used in mythological scenes, and also as part of the festivities associated with the marriage between two people. Furthermore, in the ruins of sites where the Maya buried their dead, many vessels have been uncovered which have traces of cacao in them. Palka says it is unclear whether people were simply buried with their pots, or if the pots were a part of the rituals for a person's funeral. This is something scientists are still investigating.

When the Spanish and other Europeans began to arrive in the 15th and 16th centuries, they observed the Maya drinking large amounts of chocolate, and understood that the drink was an ancient medicine. But according to Lavis, cacao was just a component of their diet, and the Maya simply knew it was good for them, just like other staple foods.

Since 2013, research has also come up with some interesting findings. It seems that in addition to its ritualistic role, cacao also served simpler functions in some early American civilizations. Palka maintains that cacao beans were adopted as currency, and the seeds were so valuable that fake ones made of clay have been found.

Archaeologist Eleanor Harrison-Buck, however, thinks that the reason why chocolate became so important was because it was harder to grow compared to plants like maize and cactus. The successful production of cacao trees needed an area of limited sun, but also plenty of humidity and lots of shade to attract the colonies of flies that pollinate the cacao trees and allow them to fruit. But the pollen, fossilized plant tissue, and botanical remains of this important crop do not preserve well in the wet, tropical environments of the Maya Lowlands where cacao was grown. As a result, archaeologists know more about the early uses of cacao than they do about ancient methods of producing the bean. To better understand how ancient civilizations produced cacao, scientist Serita Frey has been working in Belize to find out whether she can discover evidence of ancient cacao trees deep down in the soil, which she is digging up from along river banks and around important Mayan sites. By analyzing this, she hopes to find out exactly where cacao was produced in the Belize Valley in prehistoric times.
